sourceReviews.supportingSummary: The configuration schema reference explicitly accepts runtime in child files but ignores it, requires a top-level runtime and per-file data-source, and requires globally unique entity names. Its separate Autoentities section establishes explicit-definition precedence for MSSQL name collisions. The training summary's actual reference and credential-linked module ancestry support this exact admitted article, not arbitrary DAB documentation.

choiceReviews.rationale: The Autoentities section says an explicit entity wins when an MSSQL autoentities pattern produces the same entity name. That rule selects an entity definition, not the authoritative runtime. Here both definitions are valid and no discovery collision is reported, so it cannot explain REST availability. It would correctly resolve an explicit-versus-discovered Products collision in an MSSQL configuration, with runtime already settled.

Under Data source files, the reference designates one top-level file to manage runtime and explicitly ignores runtime supplied by children. Therefore the child's false flag does not override the parent's enabled REST runtime; the separately enabled entity and permission premises preserve access. The same rule correctly explains a parent/child disagreement about another runtime setting, rather than granting children independent service runtimes.

Entity-name uniqueness is a genuine rule across all loaded files, including files using different database connections. It constrains names rather than choosing which runtime flag is effective. The stem already establishes valid entity definitions, so this rule cannot cause the described enabled endpoint. It would correctly diagnose a different deployment in which two referenced files both declare the entity Order.

The multiple-configuration rules do require each file to contain data-source. That requirement addresses database connectivity and is already satisfied for both files here. It does not give the child authority over global REST configuration. The literal rule would be the relevant correction when a referenced file declares entities but omits its own data-source, even though the parent supplies a connection.
